extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, paleontologists, and graduate students studying disciplinary autonomy and macroevolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether paleontology qualifies as an autonomous scientific discipline by applying an evolutionary model that asks (1) whether the field addressed scientific problems in high demand and (2) whether it possessed a unique, privileged perspective for disclosing and explaining relevant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / demand of scientific problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the extinction and related phenomena were important scientific problems whose solution was in high demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model of disciplinary autonomy rests on (1) whether the extinction and phenomena related to extinction were important scientific problems whose solution was in high demand. Importance can be judged by connection to high-interest features of evolution (e.g., diversity, major radiations) and by whether solving them would significantly change understanding of evolution (Maynard Smith's remark that paleontology's work on extinction 'the greatest impact' on mechanisms of evolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique ability / privileged perspective to disclose facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether paleontology had a unique ability to disclose the facts of extinction and related phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second axis of the autonomy model asks whether paleontology had a privileged evidential/theoretical base uniquely well suited for solving those problems. Examples: only paleontologists have direct access to the fossil record (what died, where, when), so paleontology could 'disclose, predict, and explain the facts related to patterns in extinction and diversity across time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical plausibility and fit to evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of extinction (or any theory) must be empirically plausible and be able to make sense of the relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nature of extinction is framed as an empirical question 'to be decided by the plausibility of each of the models, combined with the ability of each to make sense of the relevant evidence.' The long-lived hegemony of an earlier model is undermined if it fails to fit empirical patterns (e.g., Darwinian model failing to explain fossil patterns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory scope / scale (ability to explain higher-order extinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful model must explain extinction patterns across taxonomic hierarchies, including simultaneous loss of many genera, families, orders, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raup's critique: random/species-level processes cannot plausibly annihilate many higher-order taxa simultaneously. A model like 'wanton extinction' is favored because it can account for extermination of many higher-order taxa and biases in extinction rates, and because only such mechanisms plausibly trigger the large-scale origination/ recovery patterns seen after mass extinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic / statistical plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorized mechanisms should not rely on extraordinarily improbable sequences of events to account for observed patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses probability examples (e.g., genus with 10 species each with 50% extinction chance yields only 0.01% chance of genus extinction by random kill-off) to argue that explanations requiring many simultaneous fortunate coincidences (e.g., many independent large-scale invasions) are implausible and thus deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsicality / privileged evidential position
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a field's problems and methods are intrinsic to the discipline because its evidence or methods are uniquely situated to address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'intrinsicality condition' is satisfied when paleontology's unique access to the fossil record privileges it for explaining extinction and diversity. This helps justify disciplinary autonomy because the field can disclose facts (and thus solve problems) that others cannot, at least with current methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to generate testable and irreducible theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to produce testable, non-reducible general theories about patterns in the history of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gould's 'Master Argument' for autonomy emphasized paleontologists as 'generators of testable and irreducible theories about pattern in the history of life.' The text treats the production of such theories (or failure to do so) as relevant to claims of autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness / lawmaking strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the field's methods/strategies produce general laws, nomothetic regularities, and fruitful research programs that organize disparate empirical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'fruitful lawmaking strategy' (e.g., species-as-particles approach) is valued because it organizes otherwise intractable biological facts (extinction, diversity) and produces general, higher-order explanations that shape future inquiry. Autonomy is tied to the field's ability to develop such lawlike accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour in standards for demonstrating adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: More demanding evidential and inferential standards for claiming adaptation or adaptive explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gould's efforts produced 'a more demanding standard for demonstrating adaptation and an interest in causes of suboptimal design.' Evaluative practice should therefore require careful, stringent evidence before accepting adaptive explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuineness of the scientific problem (problem-identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed phenomena or named processes must identify real, substantive scientific problems rather than pseudoprocesses or artifacts of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique of 'punctuated equilibrium' is that the phrase may refer to a 'pseudoprocess' and thus fails to identify a genuine scientific problem. Evaluations should ask whether a proposed phenomenon truly constitutes a well-defined, addressable problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-as-particles abstraction (appropriateness of idealization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of treating species as particles (ignoring individual peculiarities) to explain large-scale extinction and diversity patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The species-as-particles problem-solving strategy succeeds insofar as it allows paleontologists to explain macroevolutionary patterns by assuming that 'peculiarities of individual taxa do not matter.' The criterion is whether that abstraction yields explanatory and predictive success for the target phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly over explanatory resources as sufficient for autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical control or monopoly over the available evidential/theoretical resources for a problem can justify disciplinary autonomy even absent formal irreducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that autonomy does not require proving irreducibility; it is enough that, 'for whatever reason, the field has a monopoly' over explanatory resources (e.g., fossil evidence) and thus can do what no other group can do in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to central evolutionary questions (relevance to broader theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether solving the problem contributes to central issues in evolutionary theory (e.g., mechanisms of diversification, patterns of diversity through time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extinction's importance is partly measured by its ability to explain central phenomena (taxonomic radiations, standing diversity); problems that illuminate core theoretical debates are higher priority and help justify a discipline's significance.
